plain: A retirement account you pay into with money you have already paid taxes on. Later, qualified withdrawals are generally tax-free. It is not tied to an employer.

A retirement account that holds money moved out of a former employer's retirement plan, such as a 401(k). Moving the money this way is called a rollover. The account is yours, not your old employer's.
An investment account where you can hold investments like stocks, bonds, and funds. It is not a retirement account, so there are usually no age-based rules for taking money out.
The person or organization you name to receive the money in an account if you pass away. You can usually change it with a form.
Moving money or investments from one account to another. A transfer by itself is not a withdrawal.
Taking money out of an account so you can use it. From a retirement account, a withdrawal may have tax effects, which an advisor can walk through with you.
The formal word for money paid out to you from a retirement account. 'Distribution' and 'withdrawal' are often used to mean the same thing.
After a certain age, the government requires you to take a minimum amount out of some retirement accounts each year. The exact rules depend on your situation.
A professional who helps you plan and make decisions about your money and accounts. Your advisor can explain choices; you make the final decisions.
A person you choose whom the firm may contact if there are concerns about your account or they cannot reach you. A trusted contact cannot make transactions for you.
